text: Work and kinetic energy. Work. In physics, work isn't just about what makes you tired or fatigued. It has a special definition, which is when energy is transferred to an object due to the work done on it. Work is done when a force acts on something that undergoes a displacement from one position to another. Forces can vary as a function of position and displacements can be along various paths between two points. We define the increment of work, dw, done by a force vector f, acting through an infinitimal displacement, d vector r, as the dot product of these two vectors. dw equals vector f dot d vector r equals magnitude of vector f times magnitude of d vector r times cosine theta. We can find the total work done by adding up the contributions for infinitimal displacements along a path between two positions. This uses the same dot product idea introduced in chapter 2. Work done by a force. The work done by a force is the integral of the force with respect to the displacement along the path of the displacement. W sub AB equals the integral from a to b of vector f dot d vector r. The path or line integral adds up contributions along a path. Often the path is parameterized by time, so there are time dependent functions x of t and y of t that are separable. In short, we add up all the components of the force that are parallel to the direction of the path, as shown in the course web page figure. Although we expressed the dot product using the product of magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them. If it is convenient, one could use the form of the dot product that includes the vector components. Note, recall that the vector components of force are portions of a force along a given direction. The components can be positive, negative, or zero, depending on whether the force is directed along the path or perpendicular to it. The maximum work is done either parallel, cosine zero equals one, or anti-parallel, cosine pi equals negative one, while zero work is done when the force is perpendicular to the displacement, cosine theta equals zero. The units of work are force multiplied by units of length, which in the SI system is Newton meters. This combination is called a jewel and is abbreviated capital J. In the English system, used in the US, the unit of work is the foot pound, because the unit of force is the pound, LB, and the displacement is the foot, FT. Work done by constant forces and contact forces. The simplest work to evaluate is that done by a constant magnitude force in a non-varying single direction. In this case, the work is only determined by the distance traveled. Work is an integral. Consider a rectangle of height H and a length L. If the length is divided into many N small chunks of length, change in L sub N. You can visualize that the area of the rectangle can be calculated by summing up all smaller areas. I.e. A equals the sum over N of H times change in L sub N equals H times L. The course web page figure shows two people exerting a constant force. In FIG A, the man exerts a constant force vector F along the handle of a lawnmower, where the horizontal displacement is vector D. Thus, the work done on the lawnmower is W equals vector F dot vector D equals FD cosine theta, where theta is the angle relative to the horizontal. FIG's B and C show a woman holding a briefcase. The woman must exert an upward force to balance the weight of the briefcase. In both cases, the work done is zero, because either in B, displacement is zero, or in C, the force is perpendicular to the displacement. When you mow the grass, other forces act on the lawnmower, i.e. contact force of the ground and gravitational force. For an object moving on a surface, the displacement D vector R is tangent or parallel to the surface. The normal force vector N is perpendicular or normal to the surface, i.e. theta equals 90 degrees. As a result, we have DW sub N equals vector capital N dot D vector R equals N times DR cosine 90 degrees equals zero. The normal force never does work under these circumstances. The part of the contact force on the object that is parallel to the surface is friction vector F. For an object sliding along the surface, the kinetic friction vector F sub K is opposite to D vector R, so the work done by kinetic friction is negative. We can write this as an integral by W sub F R equals integral from A to B vector F sub K dot D vector R equals minus F sub K integral from A to B DR equals minus F sub K L sub AB, where L sub AB is the path length on the surface. Checkpoint, pause and check your understanding. A box slides horizontally while gravity acts vertically downward. Does gravity do work on the box during the horizontal motion? Explain using the angle between force and displacement. The force of static friction does no work in the reference frame of the surface because the point of contact does not slip across the surface. As an external force, static friction can do work. Static friction can perform positive work to prevent someone from sliding off a sled when the sled is moving. Negative work via air resistance to balance the positive work via road on the drive wheels for a car moving down a flat highway. You need to analyze each particular case to determine the work done by the forces, whether positive, negative or zero. The gravitational force or weight of the lawnmower has a constant magnitude Mg and direction vertically down. The work done by gravity on the mower is the dot product of its weight and its displacement. It is convenient to express the x-axis along the horizontal and the y-axis vertically up. Then the gravitational force is minus Mg j-hat. So the work done by gravity Wg over any path A to B equals Wg A B equals minus Mg j-hat dot R sub B minus R sub A equals minus Mg times Y sub B minus Y sub A. The work done on an object by gravity depends only on the object's weight, Mg, and the difference in height. H equals Y sub B minus Y sub A, the object is displaced. Gravity does negative work that moves upward, i.e. Y sub B is greater than Y sub A, which means you must do positive work against gravity to lift an object upward. Alternatively, gravity does positive work on an object that moves downward, Y sub B less than Y sub A, which means that you do negative work against gravity to control the descent of the object so it doesn't drop to the ground. Example problem, work to push a lawnmower. The problem, how much work is done on the lawnmower by the person in Figure A if he exerts a constant force of 75 newtons at an angle 35 degrees below the horizontal and pushes the mower 25 meters on level ground. The work solution follows. The model. The lawnmower moves on level ground so its displacement is horizontal. The applied force has constant magnitude and direction, and the angle between the applied force and the displacement is 35 degrees. The vertical component of the applied force does not contribute to the work because the mower does not move vertically. The work is determined by the component of the applied force parallel to the displacement. The math. For a constant force acting over a straight displacement, the work done by the force is the dot product of the force and displacement, W equals FD cos theta. The work done on the lawnmower follows by evaluating the dot product using the force magnitude, displacement, and angle between them. W equals 75 newtons times 25 meters times cosine 35 degrees equals 1536 joules. The conclusion. The work done on the lawnmower by the applied force is 1500 joules. This result is positive because the applied force has a component in the same direction as the mower's displacement. The calculation uses the dot product introduced earlier, which is why only the force component parallel to the displacement transfers energy to the mower. Example problem. Moving a couch. The problem. You decide to move your couch to a new position on your horizontal living room floor. The normal force on the couch is 1 kilo Newton and the coefficient of friction is 0.6. A. You first push the couch 3 meters parallel to a wall and then 1 meter perpendicular to the wall. A to B in figure. How much work is done by the frictional force? B. You don't like the new position so you move the couch straight back to its original position. B to A in figure. What was the total work done against friction moving the couch away from its original position and back again? The worked solution follows. The model. The couch moves on a horizontal surface so the normal force is constant. The kinetic friction force has constant magnitude and always points opposite the direction of motion. Because kinetic friction is a non-conservative force, the work done by friction depends on the total path length traveled rather than only the starting and ending positions. The work done by friction is negative while the work done against friction is positive. The math. The magnitude of the kinetic friction force is determined by the coefficient of kinetic friction and the normal force. F sub k equals mu sub k n. The friction force follows from the given coefficient and normal force. F sub k equals 0.6 times 1000 newtons equals 600 newtons. A. The path from A to B consists of two straight segments so the distance traveled is the sum of their length. D sub A B equals 3 meters plus 1 meter equals 4 meters. The friction force points opposite the displacement along each segment so the work done by friction is negative. W sub F R comma A B equals negative F sub k D sub A B equals negative 600 newtons times 4 meters equals negative 2400 joules. B. The return path from B to A is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 meters and 1 meter. D sub B A equals square root of 3 meters squared plus 1 meter squared equals square root of 10 meters. The total distance traveled away from the original position and back again is the sum of the two part outbound path and the direct return path. D total equals 3 meters plus 1 meter plus square root of 10 meters. The work done against friction is positive because it is the energy supplied to overcome the negative work done by friction. W sub against equals F sub k times D sub total equals 600 newtons times 3 plus 1 plus square root of 10 meters equals 4300 joules. The conclusion. The work done by friction as the couch moves from A to B is negative 2400 joules while the total work done against friction for the round trip is 4300 joules. The negative sign in part A indicates that friction removes mechanical energy from the couch. The round trip result illustrates that friction is non-conservative because the energy lost depends on the total path length even though the couch returns to its starting position. Example problem. Shelving a book. The problem. You lift an oversized library book weighing 20 newtons, 1 meter vertically down from a shelf and carry it 3 meters horizontally to a table, figure. A. How much work does gravity do on the book? B. When you're finished, you move the book in a straight line back to its original place on the shelf. What was the total work done against gravity moving the book away from its original position on the shelf and back again? The worked solution follows. The model. The book moves under the influence of gravity which points vertically downward with constant magnitude. We choose plus J hat upward on the y-axis so a downward displacement has a negative change in height. Gravity is conservative so the work done by gravity depends only on the initial and final heights and not on the horizontal part of the path. The math. For vertical motion with plus J hat upward, the work done by gravity is determined by the weight of the book and the change in height. Work sub G equals negative W times Y sub F minus Y sub I. A. The book moves downward by 1 meter so the signed change in height is negative. Y sub F minus Y sub I equals negative 1 meter. The work done by gravity follows from the gravitational expression. W sub G equals negative 20 newtons times negative 1 meter equals 20 joules. Part B. The book begins and ends at the same height after the round trip so the net change in height is 0. Y sub F minus Y sub I equals 0. Because gravity is conservative, the total work done by gravity over the closed path is 0 and the total work done against gravity is also 0. W sub against equals 0 joules. The conclusion. The work done by gravity while the book is moved downward from the shelf to the table is 20 joules and the total work done against gravity over the complete trip away from the shelf and back is 0 joules. The positive work in part A occurs because the book's displacement has a downward component in the same direction as gravity. The 0 round trip result connects back to the model assumption that gravity is conservative so only the beginning and ending heights matter. Work done by forces that vary. Forces may vary in magnitude and direction at different points in space. Additionally, the paths between two points can be curved rather than straight. The infinitesimal work done by a variable force can be expressed in terms of the force components and the displacement along the path. DW equals vector F dot vector R which equals F sub X DX plus F sub Y Dy plus F sub Z DZ. Here the forces assumed to be a function of the position. For example, vector F of X Y Z equals F sub X I hat plus F sub Y J hat plus F sub Z K hat. And the infinitesimal displacement depends on the equation of the path or D vector R equals DX I hat plus Dy J hat plus DZ K hat. The total work is a line integral which sums the infinitesimal amounts of work along the path. The physical concept of work is straightforward. First, you calculate the work for tiny displacements and second, add them up. One very important and widely applicable variable force is described by Hooke's law or the spring force. Vector F equals negative K delta vector X where K is the spring constant and delta vector X equals Vector X minus Vector X sub equilibrium is the displacement from the spring's unstretched or equilibrium position. Forces between molecules or any system undergoing displacements from a stable equilibrium behave approximately like a spring force. To calculate the work done by a spring force we can choose the X axis along the length of the spring. As the length increases the end position of the spring moves to the right in the positive I hat direction where the equilibrium point X sub equilibrium equals zero. Conversely, as the length decreases meaning the spring compresses the end position of the spring moves to the left in the negative I hat direction. With this choice of coordinates the spring force has only an X component F sub X equals negative K X and the work done when X changes from X sub A to X sub B is work done by a spring force. W sub spring A B equals the integral from A to B of F sub X DX which equals negative K times the integral from A to B of X DX which equals negative one half K times X squared evaluated from A to B which equals negative one half K times the quantity X sub B squared minus X sub A squared. The work done by the spring W sub A B depends only on the starting and ending points A and B. It is independent of the actual path between them as long as it starts at A and ends at B. The actual path could involve going back and forth before ending. For the one-dimensional case involving the work done by a spring force you can readily see the correspondence between the work done by a force and the area under the curve of the curve. In general, a one-dimensional integral is the limit of the sum of infinitesimals represented by rectangles or strips. The web page includes the code and graph used to verify the areas using simple geometry. Example problem work done by a variable force. An object moves along a parabolic path Y equals 0.5 inverse meters times X squared from the origin A equals 0, 0 to the point B equals 2 meters, 2 meters under the action of a force vector F equals 5 nu-tons per meter I hat plus 10 nu-tons per meter J hat figure. Calculate the work done. The worked solution. The model. The object moves in the X Y plane along a prescribed parabolic path from A to B. The applied force varies with position and has both I hat and J hat components. The work is found from a line integral because both the force and the direction of the displacement can change along the path. The path equation allows the displacement component DY to be written in terms of DX. The math. For a variable force acting along a path, the infinitesimal work is the dot product between the force and infinitesimal displacement. DW equals vector F dot D vector R equals F sub X DX plus F sub Y DY. The path equation relates the vertical position to the horizontal position Y equals 0.5 inverse meters times X squared. The vertical displacement follows by differentiating the path equation with respect to X. DY equals 1.0 inverse meters times X DX. The integrand follows by replacing Y and DY in the dot product expression. DW equals 5 N per meter Y DX plus 10 N per meter X DY equals 5 N per meter times 0.5 meters to the negative first power X squared DX plus 10 N per meter times X times 1.0 meters to the negative first power X DX. Equals 12.5 N per meter X squared DX. The total work follows by integrating the infinitesimal work from X equals 0 to X equals 2 meters. W equals the integral from 0 to 2 meters of 12.5 N per meter times X cubed DX. Which equals 12.5 N per meter times X cubed over 3 evaluated from 0 to 2 meters, which equals 33.3 joules. The conclusion. The work done by the variable force along the parabolic path is 33 joules. The result depends on the path because the force varies with position and the displacement direction changes along the curve. This example extends the constant force dot product idea by showing how work is accumulated from many small dot products along a curved trajectory. Example problem. Work done by a spring force. The problem. A perfectly elastic spring requires 0.54 joules of work to stretch 6 centimeters from its equilibrium position as in figure B. A. What is its spring constant K? B. How much work is required to stretch it an additional 6 centimeters. The worked solution follows. The model. The spring obeys Hooke's law so the force exerted by the spring is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and points opposite that displacement. The work required to stretch the spring is the work done against the spring force. Because the spring force is conservative, the work depends only on the initial and final displacements from equilibrium. Centimeters are kept as the displacement unit because the problem is simpler when the spring constant is reported in N over centimeters. The math. The work required to stretch a spring from XA to XB is the positive work done against the spring force. W equals 1.5 K X sub B squared minus X sub A squared. A. For the first stretch, the spring moves from equilibrium to X sub B equals 6 centimeters. So X sub A equals 0. Since one joule equals 100 Newton centimeters, the given work is 0.54 joules equals 54 Newton centimeters. The spring constant follows by solving the spring work expression for K. K equals 2W over X sub B squared minus X sub A squared equals 2 times 54 Newton centimeters over 6 centimeters squared minus 0 centimeters squared. K equals 3 Newton's per centimeter B. For the additional stretch, the spring moves from X sub A equals 6 centimeters to X sub B equals 12 centimeters. The required work follows by reusing the spring work expression with the spring constant from part A. W equals 1.5 times the quantity 3 Newton's per centimeter times 12 centimeters squared minus 6 centimeters squared equals 162 Newton centimeters equals 1.62 joules. The conclusion. The spring constant is 3 Newton's per centimeter and the work required to stretch the spring an additional 6 centimeters is 1.6 joules. The second stretch requires more work than the first equal length stretch because the spring force grows with displacement from equilibrium. This result connects the area under the curve interpretation of work to the quadratic dependence of spring work on displacement.

The work is found from a line integral because both the force and the direction of the displacement can change along the path. The path equation allows the displacement component DY to be written in terms of DX.
The math. For a variable force acting along a path, the infinitesimal work is the dot product between the force and infinitesimal displacement.
DW equals vector F dot D vector R equals F sub X DX plus F sub Y DY. The path equation relates the vertical position to the horizontal position Y equals 0.5 inverse meters times X squared.

The vertical displacement follows by differentiating the path equation with respect to X. DY equals 1.0 inverse meters times X DX. The integrand follows by replacing Y and DY in the dot product expression.

DW equals 5 N per meter Y DX plus 10 N per meter X DY equals 5 N per meter times 0.5 meters to the negative first power X squared DX plus 10 N per meter times X times 1.0 meters to the negative first power X DX.

Equals 12.5 N per meter X squared DX. The total work follows by integrating the infinitesimal work from X equals 0 to X equals 2 meters. W equals the integral from 0 to 2 meters of 12.5 N per meter times X cubed DX.
Which equals 12.5 N per meter times X cubed over 3 evaluated from 0 to 2 meters, which equals 33.3 joules. The conclusion. The work done by the variable force along the parabolic path is 33 joules.

The result depends on the path because the force varies with position and the displacement direction changes along the curve. This example extends the constant force dot product idea by showing how work is accumulated from many small dot products along a curved trajectory.
Example problem. Work done by a spring force. The problem. A perfectly elastic spring requires 0.54 joules of work to stretch 6 centimeters from its equilibrium position as in figure B.
A. What is its spring constant K? B. How much work is required to stretch it an additional 6 centimeters. The worked solution follows.

The model. The spring obeys Hooke's law so the force exerted by the spring is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and points opposite that displacement. The work required to stretch the spring is the work done against the spring force.
Because the spring force is conservative, the work depends only on the initial and final displacements from equilibrium.
Centimeters are kept as the displacement unit because the problem is simpler when the spring constant is reported in N over centimeters. The math.
The work required to stretch a spring from XA to XB is the positive work done against the spring force. W equals 1.5 K X sub B squared minus X sub A squared. A.

For the first stretch, the spring moves from equilibrium to X sub B equals 6 centimeters. So X sub A equals 0. Since one joule equals 100 Newton centimeters, the given work is 0.54 joules equals 54 Newton centimeters.

The spring constant follows by solving the spring work expression for K. K equals 2W over X sub B squared minus X sub A squared equals 2 times 54 Newton centimeters over 6 centimeters squared minus 0 centimeters squared.

K equals 3 Newton's per centimeter B. For the additional stretch, the spring moves from X sub A equals 6 centimeters to X sub B equals 12 centimeters. The required work follows by reusing the spring work expression with the spring constant from part A.

W equals 1.5 times the quantity 3 Newton's per centimeter times 12 centimeters squared minus 6 centimeters squared equals 162 Newton centimeters equals 1.62 joules. The conclusion. The spring constant is 3 Newton's per centimeter and the work required to stretch the spring an additional 6 centimeters is 1.6 joules.

The second stretch requires more work than the first equal length stretch because the spring force grows with displacement from equilibrium. This result connects the area under the curve interpretation of work to the quadratic dependence of spring work on displacement.
